stem: A healthcare worker cannot achieve an adequate fit with a required tight-fitting respirator. Which alternative does not require fit testing?

options.A: A NIOSH-approved loose-fitting PAPR with a hood or helmet appropriate for the hazard.
options.B: A surgical mask used as equivalent protection for any airborne hazard.
options.C: A tight-fitting PAPR used without fit testing.
options.D: No respiratory protection if an N95 fit test cannot be passed.

rationale: NIOSH states that loose-fitting powered air-purifying respirators (PAPRs), including loose-fitting hoods or helmets, do not require fit testing because they do not depend on a tight facial seal. Tight-fitting respirators, including tight-fitting PAPRs, do require fit testing. A is correct when the selected PAPR is appropriate for the hazard and respiratory-protection program.
educational_objective: Distinguish loose-fitting PAPRs from tight-fitting respirators with respect to fit-testing requirements.
source_locator: Fit Testing — Overview; PAPR — Overview/What to know
source_claim_supported: Loose-fitting PAPRs do not require fit testing; tight-fitting respirators do.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — appropriate PPE and respiratory protection
blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — respirator selection

source_original.stem: A nurse cannot use a tight-fitting N95 respirator because an adequate fit cannot be achieved. Which respiratory-protection alternative can avoid the same fit-testing requirement?

options.A: Use a loose-fitting hood or helmet PAPR when a tight-fitting respirator cannot be fit-tested
options.B: Use a surgical mask as equivalent respiratory protection for a highly transmissible airborne infection
options.C: Use a tight-fitting PAPR without fit testing because every PAPR is exempt from fit testing
options.D: Provide no respiratory protection when an employee cannot pass an N95 respirator fit test

source_original.rationale: NIOSH distinguishes tight-fitting from loose-fitting PAPRs. Tight-fitting respirators require fit testing, whereas a loose-fitting PAPR hood or helmet does not depend on a tight facial seal and therefore does not require fit testing.
source_original.source_detail: 2025 guidance: tight-fitting respirators require fit testing; loose-fitting PAPRs with hoods/helmets do not; published 2025-02-03; accessed 2026-08-14.

correction_summary: Added the requirement that the loose-fitting PAPR be appropriate for the hazard and NIOSH-approved, retained the exact NIOSH fit-testing distinction, and reduced difficulty to medium.

audit_findings.claim_audit: Loose-fitting versus tight-fitting fit-test distinction directly supported.

distractor_audit.C: False; tight-fitting PAPRs require fit testing.
distractor_audit.D: Unsafe and contrary to respiratory protection requirements.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: A is the only fit-test-exempt respiratory alternative presented.
audit_findings.blueprint: PPE selection fits Safety and Infection Prevention and Control.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked NIOSH Fit Testing and PAPR pages; A remains unique.
